title: 道德經 第四十三章
source: Laozi 老子, 道德經 (Daodejing), chapter 43, in the Wang Bi 王弼 recension (華亭張氏原本, 晉 王弼注), as transcribed at Chinese Wikisource; verified character-for-character against the printed public-domain edition of Paul Carus, Lao-Tze's Tao-Teh-King: Chinese-English (Chicago: Open Court, 1898), p. 74. All punctuation is editorial — the original has none — and the division into 81 chapters is traditional. Sense-units follow Wang Bi's own commentary lemmata. Translations are made fresh from the Chinese. Pronunciation convention: modern Mandarin, given in Hanyu Pinyin — an admitted anachronism, and the living convention for reading these texts. Where an Old Chinese rhyme is invisible in Mandarin, a note says so. Prepared audio is synthesized speech in that same convention (cmn-CN-Chirp3-HD-Achernar).
about: Chapter 43 of the Daodejing. Its traditional title is 徧用 (Universal Use). The chapter titles are not part of the text and are not Wang Bi's: they come from the Heshanggong 河上公 recension and are carried here only as navigation labels, so a chapter can be found by something other than its number. The received text is Wang Bi's (3rd c. AD); the manuscripts found at Mawangdui (1973) and Guodian (1993) are older and differ in places, and the notes flag those differences where they matter. Classical Chinese has no inflection, no obligatory subject, and no fixed parts of speech — the notes show how the line produces its meaning. Read the characters; the pinyin under each one is a reading aid you can hide with the transcription button.

sentences.t:
天下之至柔，
馳騁天下之至堅。

morph.gloss: all under heaven — the whole inhabited world and everyone in it
the utmost, the most ——: a superlative standing before its adjective
to gallop, to ride hard over — a horse given its head across open country
to gallop, to drive a horse hard
to give a horse its head, to range unchecked
all under heaven — the whole inhabited world and everyone in it
hard, firm, unyielding — of stone and metal

sentences.l:
The softest thing under heaven
gallops over the hardest thing under heaven.
sentences.i: The most yielding thing under heaven rides down the most unyielding thing under heaven.
sentences.n:
至 before an adjective makes a superlative: 至柔 'the utmost soft', 至堅 'the utmost hard'. Both are bare adjectives used as nouns — the softest *thing* — with nothing marking the shift but the 之 in front and the position.

Neither thing is named. The soft one is water, as chapter 78 will say outright: 天下莫柔弱於水, nothing under heaven is softer than water, and yet nothing beats it at attacking the hard. Wang Bi adds a second candidate — breath, which gets in everywhere, as water gets everywhere. Leaving the subject unstated is not vagueness; it lets the line be about anything soft.

馳騁 is a violent verb for a gentle argument, and that is the joke. It is a war word: chariots let loose across a plain. Chapter 12 used it of hunting — 馳騁畋獵令人心發狂, riding hard at the chase drives men's hearts mad. Water is here doing what cavalry does.

sentences.t:
無有入無間，
吾是以知無為之有益。

morph.gloss: substance, what there is of a thing
a crack, a crevice — the chink between two things that are shut together. Read jiàn in this sense; jiān, the reading in chapter 5's 天地之間, is 'the space between'
therefore — a fused connective, which neither 是 'this' nor 以 'by means of' gives you alone
acting without forcing — action that adds no force of its own
the subordinating particle — it turns the whole clause 無為有益 ('acting without forcing has benefit') into a noun, 'that acting without forcing has benefit'. Not the genitive 'of' this time

sentences.l:
What has no substance enters where there is no gap;
by this I know the benefit there is in acting without forcing.
sentences.i: The substanceless gets in where there is no crack; from this I know what is to be gained by acting without forcing.
sentences.n:
無有入無間 is five characters and is parsed two ways. Take 無有 as a noun phrase, 'that which has no substance', and the line reads as it does above. Take 無有 as a predicate — 'having nothing [to it]' — and it becomes 'because it has nothing, it enters where there is no gap'. The sense comes out much the same, which is why the argument has never had to be settled; but the grammar really is undecided, and it is worth seeing that a sentence can be that short and still be ambiguous.

無為之有益 is not 'the benefit of 無為' with 之 as 'of'. 之 here comes between a subject and its predicate — 無為 'acting without forcing' and 有益 'has benefit' — and makes the whole statement into a noun, the thing that is known. The same 之 did the same job in chapter 42's 人之所惡.

有 and 無 were made into nouns three chapters ago — chapter 40's 有生於無, what-is born of what-is-not — and they are doing it again. Nothing marks it. Position does.

Wang Bi's comment joins this line to the one before it: what is void and yielding gets through everywhere, and from that fact the usefulness of not forcing can be inferred. Notice the shape of the argument — 吾是以知, 'and this is how I know'. It is an inference from an observation, not a revelation, and the book makes this move often.

sentences.t:
不言之教，
無為之益，
天下希及之。

morph.gloss: of — genitive, tying the phrase 'no-speaking' to 'teaching'
jiào: teaching, instruction (the noun; jiāo is the verb)
all under heaven — the whole inhabited world and everyone in it
seldom, rarely — the same word that means 'too faint to hear'
to reach, to come as far as
them — the object pronoun, standing for the two things just named

sentences.l:
The teaching that says nothing,
the benefit of acting without forcing —
few under heaven reach them.
sentences.i: Teaching without words, and the gain that comes of acting without forcing: under heaven, few get as far as these.
sentences.n:
不言之教 is a phrase from chapter 2, where it was what the sage does: 處無為之事，行不言之教, he keeps to the business of not forcing and carries out the teaching of no-words. Here the two halves of that couplet come back as a pair of nouns, and the chapter ends by counting how many people manage them.

希 is the character chapter 14 gave to what is too faint to be heard, and chapter 41 used two chapters ago in 大音希聲. Here it is simply 'seldom' — the same word, sparse in time rather than in sound, as in chapter 23's 希言自然, 'few words are what is so of itself'. Sparseness is the root sense and the inaudible faintness grew out of it.

天下希及之 could be the flat observation it looks like, or a complaint. The book's habit is to state the count and let the reader supply the tone.
